title: Should we expect students to follow our methods?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino opens with a jigsaw-puzzle analogy and two classroom scenarios in science in which students reach correct answers without using the taught method. She asks whether teachers should insist on the modelled procedure or let shortcuts pass. Her answer, on balance, is that they should insist, with room for acceptable alternatives when the task allows. She gives five reasons: there may be more than one valid way, repeated use forms habits, standard methods make errors easy to spot, methods exist to help students, and novices differ from experts. The expertise point carries most weight, since experts can drop scaffolds only because they have internalised the steps. The piece is practical, grounded in explicit instruction and worked examples, and honest about its caveats.
points: Insisting on taught methods is justified because repeated use automates procedures and frees attention for content.
Standardised student working makes errors far quicker for teachers to spot and fix.
Teachers should explain why a method is used so students see it as a help rather than an arbitrary rule.
Novice-versus-expert reasoning explains the risk: students abandoning a method before they are expert may lack the underlying thinking.
The answer is not absolute, as alternative methods that give the same correct outcome can be acceptable where the task allows.
quotes: And habit formation means the steps are automated and the focus is on the content itself rather than on the method. If students don’t get into the habit of using a procedure every time, its use doesn’t get automated and it isn’t as easy for students to use it in assessments.

If students use their own methods that are not standardised or if they don’t follow a procedure at all, then finding and fixing errors in their responses is almost as easy as a game of Where’s Wally? (it’s not easy at all).

The reason teachers use models and provide clear steps to procedures is so that students know how to answer certain types of questions or how to make links between concepts. They are methods that will help students- they are used for a reason. It is important to make the reason we use a certain method as clear to students as possible.

As an expert, it may be possible to use a different method or not rely on one at all. But more importantly, experts can follow these methods without thought. If I was answering the longer response question above, I wouldn’t need to write the prompts at all but I would still be thinking of causes and effects.

When our students are learning how to answer calculations or longer-response questions, having supports in place means these tasks are easier to complete. If students move away from our methods, there is a danger they are doing so before they become experts in the type of task.
At home, when completing a jigaw puzzle where the aim is doing a hobby, it may not matter how my kids choose to complete it. But what if this happens in the classroom where the aim is learning?
